content: 1. No action will ever be undertaken if every possible objection must first be addressed and resolved. 2. I am pleased to present to you A Strategic Plan for the Elimination of Tuberculosis in the United States, which outlines the necessary steps to achieve the goal of tuberculosis elimination by the year 2010, with an interim target of reducing the case rate to 3.5 per 100,000 population by the year 2000. 3. At a national conference in 1984, Dr. James O. Mason, then Director of the Centers for Disease Control, challenged the public health community to develop a strategy to eliminate tuberculosis from the United States. 4. This plan was developed by the Centers for Disease Control and the Department of Health and Human Services' Advisory Committee for the Elimination of Tuberculosis. 5. Numerous experts, both within and outside the Department, played a significant role in the development of this plan. 6. We are grateful to all those who contributed to this process. 7. I am pleased to report that the House of Delegates of the American Medical Association and the Governing Council of the American Public Health Association have passed resolutions supporting this plan. Additionally, the American Lung Association and the American College of Preventive Medicine have endorsed the goal. 8. We thank these organizations for their support and anticipate that other organizations will take similar actions in the near future. 9. 10. The Centers for Disease Control is identifying activities for both short-term and long-term implementation. 11. The plan is being distributed to a wide range of public and private organizations with the recommendation that they take similar actions. 12. In 1987, the Secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services established an Advisory Committee for the Elimination of Tuberculosis to provide recommendations for developing new technology, applying prevention and control methods, and managing state and local tuberculosis programs aimed at eliminating tuberculosis as a public health problem. 13. After review and feedback from numerous interested individuals and organizations, this plan was finalized. 14. The committee urges the nation to establish the goal of tuberculosis elimination, defined as a case rate of less than one per million population, by the year 2010, with an interim target of a case rate of 3.5 per 100,000 population by the year 2000. 15. The U.S. case rate for 1987 was 9.3 per 100,000 population. 16. Three factors make this goal realistic: 1) tuberculosis is retreating into geographically and demographically defined pockets; 2) biotechnology now has the potential to generate improved diagnostic, treatment, and prevention modalities; and 3) advancements in computer, telecommunications, and other technologies can enhance the transfer of these technologies. 17. Therefore, a three-step plan of action was developed: 1) more effective use of existing prevention and control methods, especially in high-risk populations; 2) the development and evaluation of new technologies for treatment, diagnosis, and prevention; and 3) the rapid assessment and transfer of newly developed technologies into clinical and public health practice. 18. The committee brings this plan to the attention of the medical community and the public to stimulate positive, constructive discussion and action, increase public awareness of tuberculosis, and encourage a commitment to its elimination. 19. In the past, the United States has spent hundreds of millions of dollars annually on tuberculosis treatment and control activities. 20. Unless alternative action is taken, large and unnecessary expenditures will continue indefinitely. 21. Expenditures on tuberculosis treatment may increase in the coming years due to high morbidity rates among individuals infected with HIV, the homeless, the foreign-born, the elderly, and various minority groups. 22. Furthermore, tuberculosis has the potential to spread more widely in the community. 23. The mission of all tuberculosis control programs should now be to eliminate this disease by the year 2010. 24. Strategies for eliminating tuberculosis are outlined in this document. 25. These strategies are based on the needs and responsibilities of the various groups involved in this effort. 26. The committee acknowledges that this task will not be easy and will require considerable commitment at all levels. 27. The challenge of implementing this plan is a test of our society's willingness and ability to address a serious health problem that disproportionately affects its disenfranchised members. 28. A great nation such as ours can successfully carry out this plan. 29. It is time to commit to a tuberculosis-free society.
